title: Mapping the Kitchen Before She Can Read
sensory_anchor: the kitchen layout — counter, stove, door, window — mapped before she knew the word 'map'
emotional_signature: the first map: safety is a geometry problem
body: She is ten. She walks into the grandmother's kitchen and her eyes move: door, window, counter, stove. She does not think 'exits.' She thinks: there and there. The grandmother is at the stove. The back door is to her left. The window is behind her. The child sits at the table and she is already positioned — she can see the door, the window, and the grandmother without turning her head. She did not decide to sit there. Her body placed her. The spatial mapping is installed before language. She does not know she is doing it. She will always do it. Every room she enters for the rest of her life, her eyes will move first: door, window, position, sight lines. The kitchen is where she learned to map space. It is also where she learned that mapping space is what safe people do. The grandmother never checked the exits. The stepfather's house, she checked them constantly.

title: The Stepfather's House Is a Geometry Problem
sensory_anchor: the hallway — long, one exit, his room at the end
emotional_signature: the geometry of a house that can kill you if you read it wrong
body: The hallway is long. One end opens to the living room. The other end is his room. Her room is in the middle. The bathroom is past his room. To get to the bathroom at night, she has to pass his door. She maps this geometry before she is old enough to articulate it. The hallway is a single point of failure: one path, one exit. She learns to listen for the sound of his door before she leaves her room. She learns the timing — how long between his door closing and his breathing evening out. The hallway is not a hallway. It is a geometry problem with one solution: wait until the variables are favorable, then move. She will never live in a house with a single exit again. She will never sit with her back to the only door. The geometry of that house installed itself into her body before she had words for it.

title: Every Room Is the Same Problem
sensory_anchor: the brief pause at the door of every room she enters — one second, eyes moving, body orienting
emotional_signature: automatic: the room is a geometry problem, solved in under a second
body: She walks into a restaurant. A meeting room. A hotel lobby. A school hallway. Every room is the same problem. Where are the exits? Where are the sight lines? Where is the bottleneck? Where is the dead zone? She solves it in under a second. Her eyes move: door, window, corner, position. Her body orients: maximum options, minimum exposure. She does not think about this. She does not decide to do it. It fires before conscious thought, the same way her hand fires toward a hot stove before she feels the heat. The grandmother's kitchen taught her the geometry of safe spaces. The stepfather's house taught her the geometry of unsafe ones. Together, they installed a spatial processor that runs in the background of every room she enters for the rest of her life.

title: The Org Chart Is a Floor Plan
sensory_anchor: the org chart on the wall — she sees it as a floor plan, not a hierarchy
emotional_signature: translating: this is the same problem, different domain
body: The target organization's chart is on the wall. Three divisions, one coordinator, no redundancy. She reads it as a floor plan. The coordinator is the load-bearing wall. Remove it and three sections collapse. The divisions are rooms off a single hallway — single point of failure, same as the stepfather's house. She does not need to understand what the divisions do. She needs to understand the geometry: what supports what, what depends on what, what happens when a load-bearing element is removed. An org chart is not a hierarchy. It is a floor plan. The same spatial reasoning that maps exits and sight lines maps organizational structure. The same geometry that tells her where the bottleneck is in a room tells her where the bottleneck is in an organization. She learned this in a house where the hallway was the only path.

title: She Positions Herself Like the Grandmother Positioned the Cutting Board
sensory_anchor: the school auditorium — she sits where she can see the entrance and the stage where he is
emotional_signature: the geometry of protection: maximum options, minimum exposure, same as the kitchen
body: The school auditorium. The protectee is on stage. She sits in the third row, aisle seat. She can see the entrance. She can see the stage. She can see most of the audience. The exit is four seats to her left. She did not think about this. Her body placed her, the same way it placed her at the grandmother's kitchen table. The geometry of protection is the same as the geometry of cooking: mise en place, everything within reach, everything visible, no blind spots. The grandmother did not plan where to put the cutting board. She put it where her hand would reach without looking. The granddaughter does not plan where to sit. She sits where she can see without turning. The spatial reasoning runs in both modes simultaneously. In the kitchen, it runs as domestic comfort. In the auditorium, it runs as protective surveillance. The geometry is the same.

title: Social Spaces Are Rooms
sensory_anchor: the school cafeteria — the same geometry problem, different domain
emotional_signature: mapping social geometry the same way she maps physical geometry
body: The cafeteria is a room. Who sits where is not random. The popular kids have the center table — maximum visibility, minimum exposure, same as the grandmother's kitchen counter. The outcasts are at the edges — close to exits, far from sight lines. She reads the social geometry the same way she reads the physical geometry. Who controls the center. Who is near the door. Who has their back to the room. Who is positioned to see everything without being seen. The social hierarchy is a floor plan. The spatial reasoning that maps exits and sight lines maps social positions too. She knows who has power because she can see where they sit. She knows who is uncomfortable because she can see where they've been pushed. The geometry is the same. The domain is different.

title: Information Spaces Are Rooms
sensory_anchor: the network diagram — another floor plan, same geometry
emotional_signature: the pattern fires again: this is the same problem in a different domain
body: The network diagram is on the screen. Nodes, connections, bottlenecks. She reads it as a floor plan. The database server is the load-bearing wall. The firewall is the door. The user endpoint is the entrance. Same geometry, different domain. She maps information spaces the same way she maps physical spaces: where are the exits, where are the sight lines, where is the single point of failure. The spatial reasoning that maps the stepfather's hallway maps the network topology. She does not need to understand the protocols. She needs to understand the geometry: what connects to what, what depends on what, what happens when a critical node goes down. The information space is a room. The network is a hallway. The server is a load-bearing wall. She walks through it the same way she walks through every room she has ever entered.

title: Time Is Spatial
sensory_anchor: the calendar on the fridge — past behind, future ahead, the plan is a map
emotional_signature: organizing time the same way she organizes space
body: She organizes time the way she organizes rooms. The past is behind. The future is ahead. The plan is a map. The calendar on the fridge is not a list of appointments. It is a floor plan of the week. She can see the bottlenecks (Wednesday has three things), the dead zones (Saturday morning is open), the single points of failure (if the school pickup is late, the whole afternoon collapses). She organizes the protectee's schedule the way she organizes a room: maximum options, minimum exposure, clear sight lines, two exits. Time is spatial. She thinks in maps. The calendar is a map. The schedule is a floor plan. The week is a room. She walks through it the same way she walks through every room she enters.

title: Something Has Moved
sensory_anchor: the hallway table — something has moved, she doesn't know what, but her body knows
emotional_signature: the anomaly detection that kept her alive: something is different
body: She walks into the living room and something is wrong. She does not know what. Nothing obvious. The furniture is the same. The light is the same. But something has moved. Her spatial mapping of the room is automatic and continuous. She does not consciously catalog every object. But her body knows when something has shifted. The vase is two inches to the left. The remote control is on the arm of the couch instead of the table. These are not dramatic changes. They are anomalies. In the stepfather's house, anomalies were data. A moved object meant someone had been there. A shifted chair meant he had been pacing. A door that was closed when it was usually open meant the trajectory had changed. She learned to detect anomalies before she learned what anomalies meant. The spatial map fires the anomaly detector. Something has moved.

title: Position Is Communication
sensory_anchor: where she sits in a room — always the same geometry, always communicating the same thing
emotional_signature: position is not a decision, it is an instinct
body: She sits in the same place in every room. Not the same physical place. The same geometric place. Aisle seat. Sight lines to entrance and exit. Maximum options. Minimum exposure. She does not decide this. Her body places her. In the school auditorium, it is the third row. In a restaurant, it is the corner facing the door. In the director's office, it is the chair that lets her see both the door and the window. Position is communication. Where she sits tells the room: I see you. I have options. I am not trapped. In the stepfather's house, position was survival. In the grandmother's kitchen, position was comfort. In the field, position is operational. In the protectee's school, position is protection. The geometry is the same. The domain is different.
